<document>
# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

response:
## What the review reports

This is a pre-registered systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 studies (1998–2025, about 41,000 workers). Each study cut scheduled hours by at least 10% at full pay and measured output.

**Pooled results**
- Output per hour: +13.4% (CI 8.1 to 19.0). Heterogeneity is very high (I² 81%), and the prediction interval runs from −4% to +34%.
- Output per worker: −1.8% (CI −4.9 to +1.4).

**Moderators**
- **Weaker designs give larger gains.** Uncontrolled designs, scheduled-hours denominators and manager-reported output all yield larger per-hour gains. These three features overlap heavily across studies, which the review acknowledges.
- **Coverage-bound work loses output.** Output per worker fell about 9%, consistently across seven studies (I² 22%). Discretionary work was flat.
- **Other estimates.** Controlled discretionary studies give +9.6% per hour, and adjusting for small-study effects gives +9.1%.

**Duration, mechanisms and wellbeing**
- Four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months show +14.0%. The review concludes that effects don't decay and that novelty "can be set aside."
- At study level, the fatigue–gain correlation is weak (r = 0.18), and the meetings mechanism can't be assessed.
- Sick leave and turnover fell wherever they were reported.

**Discussion**
- The corrected estimates "converge" on a per-hour gain of about 8–10%.
- Varga & Holm's "entirely an artifact" claim is rejected, and so is Halden's "sector-general" claim.

## Overall assessment

This is careful work, and most of its claims are held at the right weight. It reports the prediction interval, not just the confidence interval. It says plainly that its moderators can't be separated. It gives the controlled-discretionary estimate so the headline +15.1% isn't over-read. It rejects both the inflated position (Halden) and the deflated one (Varga & Holm).

The subgroups are also internally coherent. Comparing per-worker and per-hour estimates gives implied hours reductions of about 11% in actual-hours studies, 15% in scheduled-hours studies and 11–12% in controlled studies. The actual-hours figure matches Varden (13–17%) and Halden's time-tracking data (14%).

There is one clear overreach, and a few points where the evidence is weaker than the text implies.

## The main problem: the duration claim

"Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside" appears in both the Results and the Abstract. It closes a question the evidence leaves open, for four reasons.

1. **It compares studies, not time points.** Four long studies having estimates similar to 19 short ones says nothing about whether effects decline *within* a study. Those four may differ in design, setting and measurement. If they are mostly uncontrolled or use scheduled hours, their inflated estimates would mask any decay. The review should report their design and measurement composition.
2. **Long follow-up selects for success.** Schemes reach 30 months mainly because they worked. Failing schemes revert early, as Halden's withdrawals did. A survivor-biased subgroup can't test for decay.
3. **The interval is wide.** +6.2 to +22.4 is consistent with no decay and also with a meaningful decline from early effects.
4. **The right test is within-study.** It needs studies that report output at several time points, analysed as a trajectory. If few studies report this, the honest conclusion is that duration is untested.

A defensible version would read: *"Four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months report gains similar to the overall estimate; this does not rule out decay, which requires within-study trajectories that few studies report. Whether gains persist remains open."*

This also matters for the Discussion. The review rejects Varga & Holm on the grounds that controlled and actual-hours studies "avoid the problems that re-analysis identified." They avoid the measurement and selection problems, but not novelty, which was Varga & Holm's third argument. The rejection of "entirely an artifact" still holds, because Varga & Holm showed novelty was possible, not that it was present. But it should rest on that point, not on the duration analysis.

## Other points

**1. The "convergence" is partly the same studies counted several times.**
Controlled, actual-hours, record-based and bias-adjusted subsets overlap heavily. Agreement among them is not four independent confirmations. Each subset also still contains studies with the other weaknesses: a controlled study may use scheduled hours, for example. The cleanest estimate would come from studies that are controlled *and* measure actual hours *and* use records. Even with k = 3–5, report it. It may fall below 8%.

**2. The small-study adjustment may be correcting the wrong thing.**
Small studies here are likely to be the uncontrolled pilots, so funnel asymmetry may reflect design rather than publication bias. Trim-and-fill is also unreliable at I² = 81%. Two analyses would help:
- Egger's test, or a PET-PEESE regression, with design as a covariate.
- A contour-enhanced funnel plot.

Without these, "evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published" is one explanation among several.

**3. Two specific studies need to be coded transparently.**
- **Halden.** Which figures were used: the original 23.4% (scheduled hours, manager index, survivors), or Varga & Holm's microdata corrections? The protocol prefers actual hours "where a study reported" them. Halden didn't report actual hours, but the re-analysis did. With 2,940 workers, Halden may carry substantial weight, so this choice matters.
- **Varden.** It has a discretionary stratum and a coverage-bound stratum. If it entered as one "mixed" study, its clearest evidence on work type is lost. If it entered as two, the entries share a context and are not independent, and the k counts in Table 1 should say so.

**4. The size of the reduction is not examined.**
Inclusion begins at a 10% cut. Per-hour gains measured against scheduled hours scale with the size of the cut. Gains measured against actual hours may scale too, through utilisation and the dropping of low-value tasks. Reduction size should be a moderator, or at least reported for each subgroup.

**5. Sick-leave figures need the same scheduling check as before.**
In four-day designs, sick leave counted in days falls about 20% even if the rate per scheduled day is unchanged. "Fell in all 14" with a pooled −31% needs per-scheduled-day figures, or a split by schedule type, before it can be read as a health effect.

**6. The fatigue correlation is weaker evidence than its placement suggests.**
An r of 0.18 across 11 studies is a between-study correlation with very little power. It doesn't count against fatigue as a mechanism within workplaces. The text doesn't overclaim, but it should say outright that this neither supports nor rules out the fatigue mechanism.

**7. The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work may not be productivity.**
As in Varden, shorter staffing during unchanged opening hours raises utilisation: fewer idle minutes and longer queues. "The per-hour gain … was real" should say what it is real *as*. It may be paid for by customers' waiting time rather than produced by workers. The recommendation to add staff follows either way.

## Where the evidence now stands

| Question | Status after the review |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain exists | Supported: roughly 8–10% in better-designed studies, possibly lower in the cleanest subset |
| Halden's 20%+ figure | Explained by design and measurement features; not representative |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Not supported for measurement and selection; novelty still untested |
| Coverage-bound work loses output | Settled: −9%, consistent across 7 studies |
| Discretionary output per worker | Roughly maintained; controlled estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2) |
| Persistence | Open; the review's duration analysis can't close it |
| Mechanism | Open; fatigue evidence weak, meetings untested, Varden's 24-month test pending |

I can draft these points as a referee report, or write suggested replacement text for the Abstract and the Duration section.
